sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
A typical op-amp has a single dominant pole, so its open-loop gain is flat at \(A_0\) up to a low corner \(\omega_{-3dB}\) and then falls at \(-20\) dB/decade until it reaches 1 at the **unity-gain frequency** \(\omega_u\). On that slope, gain times frequency is constant, which is why \(\omega_u\) is also called the **gain–bandwidth product**.

Close the loop with feedback factor \(f\) and the closed-loop gain is about \(1/f\) out to the frequency where the open-loop curve drops to meet it. Asking for more closed-loop gain means less bandwidth, and vice versa: the product is roughly fixed.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ A(j\omega) = \frac{A_0}{1 + j\omega/\omega_{-3dB}}, \qquad \omega_u \approx A_0\,\omega_{-3dB} \]
Closed loop with feedback \(f\):
\[ A_{CL}(j\omega) \approx \frac{1/f}{1 + j\omega/(f\,\omega_u)}, \qquad \omega_{CL} \approx f\,\omega_u = \frac{\omega_u}{A_{CL,0}} \]

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
An op-amp has \(A_0 = 2\times10^5\) and \(\omega_{-3dB} = 2\pi\times5\ \mathrm{Hz}\), so \(f_u \approx 1\ \mathrm{MHz}\). Configured for a gain of 25:
\[ f_{CL} \approx \frac{1\ \mathrm{MHz}}{25} = 40\ \mathrm{kHz} \]
Splitting the gain into two stages of 5 each gives 200 kHz per stage. The cascade's overall bandwidth is somewhat less than 200 kHz, but still much wider than 40 kHz.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Using the noise gain versus signal gain inconsistently; GBW applies to \(1/f\).
- Confusing \(\omega_{-3dB}\) (open-loop, tiny) with the closed-loop bandwidth.
- Mixing Hz and rad/s when quoting GBW.
- Expecting GBW to hold for op-amps with significant second poles.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The gain-bandwidth trade-off frames op-amp selection, closed-loop settling time and stability. More loop gain at high frequency also brings the extra poles closer to crossover.
